title: Yudhishthira on the riverbank
hookLine: the war is won, the funeral rites are done, and the new king falls down on the riverbank and can't get up
carry: mourning has its days; then dharma calls you up
tomorrow: Arjuna has forgotten the Gita. what will Krishna do?

lines: THE KING FALLS ON THE BANK.
THE BLIND KING SAYS: GET UP.
cards: The water offerings for Bhishma have been poured into the Ganga. The great teacher is gone. Yudhishthira has listened to him at length, about kingship, duty and peace.
He has the crown and the kingdom. And at the riverbank, in Ganguli's telling, he simply goes down, collapsing on the bank, overwhelmed by grief. Bhima holds him.
Krishna speaks to him. And the old blind king Dhritarashtra, whose own sons died in this war, is the one who tells him to get up. A new book opens with a king on the ground.

teach.b: Ashvamedhika is the book of the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice: a great royal rite in which a consecrated horse wanders free, guarded by warriors. The idea isn't Yudhishthira's.
He wants to leave the throne for the forest. It's the sage Vyasa who tells him grief can't be the whole of a king's life.
Perform sacrifices, Vyasa says, give gifts, take up your work; the horse sacrifice will cleanse what weighs on you. Yudhishthira's answer is practical.
The war has emptied the treasury, and he will not squeeze grieving people for more.
So Vyasa points to old King Marutta, whose sacrifice in the Himalayas was so lavish that the gold left behind is still there. Go and bring it. Here's the Hindu shape underneath.
Grief is given real room: the water offerings, the days of rites, the family sitting together. But it has a shape and an end.

teach.h: MOURNING HAS ITS DAYS, THEN DHARMA CALLS
teach.b: Many Hindu families keep ten to thirteen days of mourning after a death, closed with a ceremony, and then the household goes back to its work, its pujas, its festivals. The return isn't forgetting.
It's dharma calling the living back up, and it often begins, as Vyasa says, with giving: feeding guests and priests, gifts in the name of the one who died.
The book of the horse begins on the ground, with a blind king who lost every son telling the winner to stand.

how: The Ashvamedhika Parva is the book of the Mahabharata that follows Bhishma's teachings; Hindus hear it in recitations of the full epic, and the horse sacrifice is remembered as a great royal rite of the Vedic world.

o: a prayer said over a king's war horse
the stables where royal horses are kept
the book of the horse sacrifice, a royal rite

games.q: the new book opens — tap the pairs.

s: Yudhishthira proposes the horse sacrifice himself
he wants the forest; it's Vyasa who tells him to perform it.
many Hindu families close the mourning days with a ceremony
often after ten to thirteen days, and then the household returns to its pujas and its work.
the gold for the rite comes from new taxes
Vyasa points to the gold King Marutta left in the mountains.

games.q: you're Vyasa. Yudhishthira has mourned, and still wants to run to the forest. what do you tell him?
o: go. grief is a good reason to leave the throne.
keep grieving; the dead deserve nothing less.
take up a king's work again: sacrifice, give, rule.
games.why: Vyasa calls him back to dharma: the horse sacrifice, gifts, a king's work. the grief is honored, and then he's asked to stand.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've lost, or someone near you who is grieving. Breathe in and give the grief its room; nothing needs fixing. Breathe out and ask: what's one ordinary duty I could take up again, gently, in their honor?
If you pray, light a small lamp or offer it in their name; if you don't, simply hold them in mind as you do it.

wordCard.voice: Ashvamedhika. The book of the horse sacrifice, which begins with a grieving king and an empty treasury.
